newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Nedcor sees SAfrica '97 growth dipping to 2 pct.
newsitem.headline: Nedcor sees SAfrica '97 growth dipping to 2 pct.

text.p: South African economic growth is likely to slow to around two percent gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 from an estimated three percent last year, banking group Nedcor said in an economic review released on Friday.
It forecasts a slowdown in consumer spending, which accounts for about 60 percent of economic activity, due to high levels of debt hanging over from 1996.
"Fiscal policy is also likely to be contractionary, given government's commitment to reducing the deficit to four percent of GDP in fiscal 1997/98," Nedcor's economics unit said.
Prospects for a cut in the central Reserve Bank's 17-percent lending rate would depend mainly on private sector credit demand.

"Annual growth (in private sector credit demand) will have to fall towards 12 percent early in the year from the current 17 percent to allow for a cut in Bank rate late in the second quarter," it said.

The unit forecasts economic growth would slow to around two percent this year but said "a sustained upward trend should develop towards the end of 1997, assisted by firm export growth and a strong investment cycle."
Inflation was likely to stay above nine percent for the first six months but fall in the second half to an average of about 8.7 percent for 1997.

Accelerating plant expansion, modernisation and improving export performances would affect the current account of the balance of payments deficit, reducing it to around four billion rand ($867.9 million) from an estimated overall deficit of 11 billion rand in 1996.
"One of the encouraging features of the current economic upswing has been the strong rise in fixed investment spending on capital equipment," the unit said.
Nedcor's capital expenditure survey, listing capital projects valued at over 20 million rand, showed that 211 projects announced in 1996 had a combined value of 74 billion rand.
"Fixed investment is likely to remain robust during 1997 and 1998," Nedcor said.
Improving investor confidence would boost gross gold and foreign exchange reserves to around 15.5 billion rand, but more action was needed to lure additional foreign capital.

"Rapid progress on stated policy objectives therefore needs to be made to alleviate short-term pressure on the rand, but even more importantly to attract foreign capital of a more permanent and therefore stable nature," the unit said.

Nedcor analysts predicted an average rand-dollar exchange rate of 4.764 in 1997 and a rand-sterling rate of 7.966. It said gold was likely to trade at an average of $364 over the year, which would be equivalent to 1,735 rand an ounce.
